_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Putting patient records on phones or tablets, with prompts that tell health workers what to do next and text reminders to patients, should make primary care more reliable. Fewer people get missed, more turn up for vaccinations and check-ups, and health workers follow guidelines better. Most people would assume this leads to better health, especially in low-resource settings where paper systems are weak.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

outlet_unverified.sentence: We could not verify where this belief is published.

outlet_unverified.by: code: no proposed outlet verified (a model's proposals, checked by code)

what_the_sources_show.statement: The held review says digital tracking and decision-support tools have mixed results: they may lead to benefits in some situations but may make little or no difference in others, and often the full impact is not known because studies are too few or unclear.
what_the_sources_show.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.
direction.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code
direction.why: The belief expects reliable improvement in care and health, but the review finds only possible benefits in some situations and little or no difference in others, so it holds only in part.

reader_with_a_decision: Ministry of health digital-health leads, programme managers in NGOs and donor agencies, and district primary-care planners. They are deciding whether to fund, scale up, or redesign mobile tracking systems that include decision-support prompts and/or patient reminders, and which components to prioritise given limited budgets.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Randomised trials, pooled in a systematic review, show clear and consistent improvement in both the care received and health outcomes for every combination: tracking plus provider prompts, tracking plus patient reminders, and tracking plus both. The certainty would have to be moderate or high, so the popular assumption holds without important qualification.

kill_condition_tested.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code
kill_condition_tested.note: The condition is not met: the passages show mixed effects and insufficient or unclear evidence rather than clear, consistent, moderate-or-high-certainty improvement across all combinations, so the unqualified assumption is not supported.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Primary health care services in any country where health workers use mobile devices (phones or tablets) to digitally track each patient's care. The tracking is combined with on-screen decision support for health workers, targeted reminder or communication messages to patients, or both. It is compared with usual care such as paper-based records. Outcomes cover two things: whether care follows recommended practice and reaches people on time (e.g. antenatal visits, immunisation completion, treatment adherence, guideline adherence), and health outcomes for patients. It also covers unintended consequences.

out.what: Effects of patient reminder messages or decision-support tools used on their own, without digital tracking of the patient's care
out.why: The question asks about tracking combined with these components; standalone interventions are a different evidence base.

out.what: Hospital or specialist-care settings, and electronic health records on desktop systems
out.why: The question is limited to primary health care and mobile devices.

out.what: Cost-effectiveness, implementation feasibility, and health-worker or patient acceptability
out.why: These matter for adoption but are separate from whether the intervention improves care and health.

out.what: Telemedicine and remote consultations between providers, or between providers and patients
out.why: These are different digital interventions from tracking with prompts and reminders.

out.what: Data privacy and security of mobile health systems
out.why: This is an important governance question but not an effectiveness question.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Effect estimates from randomised and cluster-randomised trials comparing mobile tracking plus decision support and/or patient reminders against usual care. Examples include risk ratios or differences in antenatal care attendance, childhood immunisation completion, health-worker adherence to clinical guidelines, treatment adherence, and health outcomes such as morbidity or mortality, with their confidence intervals.
evidence_standard.assessed: The certainty-of-evidence ratings (e.g. GRADE high/moderate/low/very low) that a systematic review assigns to each outcome and intervention combination. Also the review authors' graded conclusions, such as 'probably improves' or 'may make little or no difference', and any guideline panel's judgement on recommending these interventions.
